about: Aerodynamics 1 (AERO40001) is a core, 7.5-credit Autumn-term module in Year 1 of Imperial's MEng Aeronautical Engineering (H401). It introduces the basic laws of low-speed (incompressible) fluid flow, conservation of mass and momentum and the role of viscosity, and uses control-volume analysis to explain lift, drag and boundary layers. The topic order follows the department's module descriptor as recorded when this pack was written; the public pages checked here confirm only the module's title, status, term and credits, so compare the order with your own lecture list. Imperial's public pages give no assessment breakdown for this module.

notes.h: What a fluid is, and the ideas behind Bernoulli
notes.body:
Aerodynamics 1 starts by setting up the vocabulary and assumptions used for the rest of the course. Most of the module deals with low-speed (incompressible) flow.

What is a fluid?
- A fluid is a substance that deforms continuously when a shear stress is applied, however small that stress is. A solid resists shear with a finite deformation; a fluid keeps flowing.
- Continuum hypothesis: we treat the fluid as continuous, so density, pressure and velocity are smooth functions of position and time. This holds when the length scales of interest are much larger than the molecular mean free path (about 70 nm for air at sea level, approximately).

Key properties
- Density ρ (kg/m³): about 1.225 kg/m³ for air at ISA sea level and about 1000 kg/m³ for water.
- Pressure p (Pa): a normal stress that acts equally in all directions at a point in a fluid at rest.
- Dynamic viscosity μ (Pa s): resistance to shear. For a Newtonian fluid τ = μ du/dy. Air at sea level has μ ≈ 1.79 × 10⁻⁵ Pa s. Kinematic viscosity ν = μ/ρ ≈ 1.46 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s for air.

Describing a flow
- Steady flow: properties at a fixed point do not change with time.
- Streamline: a line everywhere tangent to the local velocity. No flow crosses a streamline.
- Pathline: the path one particle actually follows. Streakline: the line of all particles that have passed through one point (what dye or smoke shows). In steady flow all three coincide.
- Incompressible flow: density is taken as constant. For air this is a good model when the Mach number is below about 0.3, where density changes are under about 5%.

Bernoulli's equation
For steady, inviscid, incompressible flow along a streamline (no work or heat added):
p + ½ρV² + ρgz = constant
In aerodynamics the ρgz term is normally negligible, so:
- static pressure p + dynamic pressure q = ½ρV² = total (stagnation) pressure p₀.
- Where the flow speeds up, static pressure falls; at a stagnation point (V = 0) the pressure equals p₀.

Worked example: air at sea level at 50 m/s has q = 0.5 × 1.225 × 50² = 1531 Pa (about 1.5 kPa). If the flow accelerates from 10 m/s to 30 m/s, the static pressure drops by ½ × 1.225 × (30² − 10²) = 490 Pa.

When Bernoulli fails
- Inside boundary layers and wakes, where viscosity matters.
- Across shock waves or where compressibility is significant.
- Across streamlines, unless the flow is irrotational (see the rotation topic).
- Through machines (fans, propellers) that add energy.

Exam tips: always state Bernoulli's assumptions before using it, and keep track of whether pressures are gauge or absolute.

notes.h: Aerofoil geometry, pressure distribution and lift
notes.body:
An aerofoil is the cross-section of a wing. Studying it in two dimensions (an infinite span) isolates the section's behaviour before three-dimensional effects are added.

Geometry
- Leading edge and trailing edge, joined by the chord line of length c.
- Camber line: halfway between upper and lower surfaces. Camber is its maximum distance from the chord line. A symmetric aerofoil has zero camber.
- Thickness: maximum thickness, usually given as a percentage of chord (for example 12%).
- Angle of attack α: angle between the chord line and the freestream.

Forces and coefficients
- The resultant aerodynamic force is split into lift L (perpendicular to the freestream) and drag D (parallel to it), plus a pitching moment M about a stated point.
- For a section, use forces per unit span: Cl = L′/(q∞c), Cd = D′/(q∞c), Cm = M′/(q∞c²), with q∞ = ½ρ∞V∞².
- For a whole wing, CL = L/(q∞S) where S is the wing area.

Pressure coefficient
Cp = (p − p∞)/q∞. In incompressible, inviscid flow Bernoulli gives Cp = 1 − (V/V∞)².
- At a stagnation point Cp = 1 (its maximum value in incompressible flow).
- Where the local speed is 1.5V∞, Cp = 1 − 2.25 = −1.25.
- Lift comes mostly from suction (negative Cp) on the upper surface; integrating the difference between lower and upper surface Cp along the chord gives Cl (for small α).

Why an aerofoil generates lift
- The sharp trailing edge forces the flow to leave smoothly (the Kutta condition). This fixes a net circulation Γ around the aerofoil.
- Kutta–Joukowski theorem: lift per unit span L′ = ρ∞V∞Γ. For example ρ = 1.225 kg/m³, V = 50 m/s and Γ = 20 m²/s give L′ = 1225 N/m.
- Explanations based on "equal transit time" are wrong: air over the upper surface actually arrives at the trailing edge before the air underneath.

Typical behaviour (approximate)
- Thin aerofoil theory gives a lift-curve slope dCl/dα = 2π per radian, about 0.11 per degree.
- A symmetric aerofoil has zero lift at α = 0; positive camber gives lift at α = 0 (a negative zero-lift angle).
- At high α the boundary layer separates from the upper surface and the aerofoil stalls: lift falls and drag rises sharply. Many conventional sections stall at roughly 12–16°, depending on shape and Reynolds number.
- Section drag at low α is mainly skin friction plus pressure (form) drag from the boundary layer.

Exam tips: define coefficients with the correct reference area or length, and remember Cp = 1 at stagnation in low-speed flow.

notes.h: The atmosphere and the International Standard Atmosphere
notes.body:
Aircraft performance and aerodynamic forces depend on air density, pressure and temperature, which change with altitude. The International Standard Atmosphere (ISA) is a reference model used to compare performance and calibrate instruments.

ISA sea-level values
- T₀ = 288.15 K (15 °C), p₀ = 101 325 Pa, ρ₀ = 1.225 kg/m³.
- Gas constant for air R = 287.05 J/(kg K), γ = 1.4, g = 9.81 m/s² (9.80665 m/s² in the formal standard).
- Speed of sound a = √(γRT) ≈ 340.3 m/s at sea level.

Layers used in this course
- Troposphere (0–11 km): temperature falls linearly with lapse rate λ = 6.5 K/km, T = T₀ − λh.
- Lower stratosphere (11–20 km): isothermal at 216.65 K (−56.5 °C).

Two governing equations
- Hydrostatic equilibrium: dp/dh = −ρg.
- Ideal gas law: p = ρRT.
Combining them: dp/p = −g dh/(RT).

Troposphere result (T = T₀ − λh):
p/p₀ = (T/T₀)^(g/(λR)), with g/(λR) ≈ 5.256
ρ/ρ₀ = (T/T₀)^(g/(λR) − 1), exponent ≈ 4.256

Isothermal layer result (T constant = T₁₁):
p = p₁₁ exp[−g(h − 11 000)/(R T₁₁)], with p₁₁ ≈ 22 632 Pa at 11 km.

Worked example: ISA at 5000 m
- T = 288.15 − 0.0065 × 5000 = 255.65 K
- p = 101 325 × (255.65/288.15)^5.256 ≈ 54 020 Pa
- ρ = p/(RT) ≈ 54 020/(287.05 × 255.65) ≈ 0.736 kg/m³
- a = √(1.4 × 287.05 × 255.65) ≈ 320.5 m/s
So density at 5 km is about 60% of the sea-level value.

Other useful values (approximate)
- 10 km: T ≈ 223.15 K, p ≈ 26.4 kPa, ρ ≈ 0.413 kg/m³, a ≈ 299.5 m/s.
- 11 km: T = 216.65 K, p ≈ 22.6 kPa, ρ ≈ 0.364 kg/m³.

Related definitions
- Density ratio σ = ρ/ρ₀.
- Pressure altitude: the ISA altitude whose pressure matches the measured pressure (what an altimeter set to 1013.25 hPa reads).
- Density altitude: the ISA altitude with the same density; on hot days it is higher than the actual altitude, which hurts take-off performance.

Exam tips: use kelvin throughout, quote the exponent 5.256 with its derivation, and check your answer is sensible (pressure roughly halves by about 5.5 km).

notes.h: Measurement techniques: pressure, velocity and flow visualisation
notes.body:
Experiments sit alongside theory in Aerodynamics 1. You need to know how the main instruments work, what they measure and their limitations.

Pressure measurement
- Static pressure tapping: a small hole drilled normal to a surface, flush with no burrs, so it senses the local static pressure without being affected by the flow speed.
- Pitot tube: an open tube facing directly into the flow. The flow stagnates inside it, so it reads total pressure p₀.
- Pitot-static tube: combines a total-pressure hole at the nose with static holes on the side. The difference gives dynamic pressure, and from incompressible Bernoulli V = √(2(p₀ − p)/ρ).
- Manometer: Δp = ρ_liquid g h, where h is the height difference of the liquid columns. An inclined manometer improves sensitivity for small pressures.
- Pressure transducers convert pressure to an electrical signal and allow fast, automated logging.

Worked example: a water manometer connected to a Pitot-static tube in a sea-level wind tunnel shows h = 30 mm.
- Δp = 1000 × 9.81 × 0.030 = 294 Pa
- V = √(2 × 294.3/1.225) ≈ 21.9 m/s

Airspeed in flight
- A Pitot-static system measures p₀ − p. If ρ₀ (sea-level density) is used instead of the local density, the result is the equivalent airspeed (EAS) rather than the true airspeed (TAS): EAS = TAS × √σ.

Velocity measurement
- Hot-wire anemometer: a very fine heated wire whose heat loss depends on the flow speed (King's law, in its simplest form E² = A + B Vⁿ with n ≈ 0.5, where E is the bridge voltage). Its fast response makes it ideal for measuring turbulent fluctuations. It must be calibrated and is fragile.
- Particle image velocimetry (PIV): the flow is seeded with small particles, illuminated twice by a laser sheet, and photographed. Cross-correlating the two images gives the velocity field over a whole plane.
- Laser Doppler anemometry: measures velocity at a point from the Doppler shift of light scattered by particles; non-intrusive.

Force measurement
- Wind-tunnel balances measure lift, drag and moments on a model directly. Drag can also be found from a wake survey (momentum deficit), covered under conservation of momentum.

Flow visualisation
- Smoke or dye show streaklines; tufts and oil-flow patterns show surface flow direction, separation and transition.

Sources of error
- Pitot probe misalignment (yaw), blockage in small tunnels, probe interference, calibration drift, and using the wrong density.
- Report measured quantities with uncertainties and propagate them through calculations.

Exam tips: be clear about which pressure each probe senses, and convert manometer heights using the manometer liquid's density, not air's.

Dimensional analysis reduces the number of variables in a problem, tells you which dimensionless groups control it and shows how to scale wind-tunnel results to full size.

Dimensions
- Use the base dimensions mass M, length L and time T. For example force [MLT⁻²], pressure [ML⁻¹T⁻²], density [ML⁻³], dynamic viscosity [ML⁻¹T⁻¹], kinematic viscosity [L²T⁻¹].
- Every physically valid equation is dimensionally homogeneous.

Buckingham Π theorem
- If a problem involves n variables built from k independent base dimensions, it can be written in terms of n − k independent dimensionless groups (Π groups).
- Method: choose k repeating variables that together contain all the base dimensions but cannot form a group on their own (commonly ρ, V and a length L). Combine each remaining variable with them and solve for exponents that make the group dimensionless.

Worked example: drag on a body
Drag F depends on ρ, V, L and μ. That is n = 5 variables and k = 3 dimensions, so there are 2 groups.
- Π₁ = F/(ρV²L²) (a force coefficient)
- Π₂ = ρVL/μ (the Reynolds number)
So F/(ρV²L²) = f(Re), or CD = f(Re) using a reference area. Add the speed of sound a and you get a third group, the Mach number M = V/a.

Important groups in aerodynamics
- Reynolds number Re = ρVL/μ = VL/ν: ratio of inertial to viscous forces. Controls boundary-layer behaviour, transition and skin friction.
- Mach number M = V/a: controls compressibility.
- Froude number Fr = V/√(gL): matters when there is a free surface.
- Force and pressure coefficients CL, CD, Cp.

Similarity
- Geometric similarity: model and full-scale shapes are identical apart from scale.
- Kinematic similarity: velocity ratios (flow patterns) match.
- Dynamic similarity: all relevant dimensionless groups (for example Re and M) match. Then the force coefficients match too.

Worked example: matching Reynolds number
A wing with chord 1.5 m flies at 60 m/s at sea level (μ ≈ 1.79 × 10⁻⁵ Pa s): Re = 1.225 × 60 × 1.5/1.79 × 10⁻⁵ ≈ 6.2 × 10⁶.
A 1/10-scale model in the same air would need 600 m/s to match Re, which would wreck Mach similarity. Practical fixes include pressurised tunnels (higher ρ), cryogenic tunnels (lower μ and higher ρ) or testing in water (ν about 15 times lower than air, so about 41 m/s would match Re here, approximately). Often only partial similarity is achieved and results are corrected.

Exam tips: show the dimension table, state n, k and the number of groups, and check each Π is dimensionless.

notes.h: Conservation of mass: control volumes and continuity
notes.body:
Conservation of mass is the first of the conservation laws in the module. It is written in two forms: an integral form for a control volume and a differential form at a point.

Control volume (integral) form
For a fixed control volume (CV) with surface S:
d/dt ∫∫∫ ρ dV + ∯ ρ(V·n) dS = 0
- The first term is the rate of increase of mass inside the CV.
- The second term is the net mass outflow through the surface (n is the outward unit normal, so inflow counts as negative).

Steady one-dimensional flow
For a stream tube or duct with one inlet and one outlet, ṁ = ρ₁A₁V₁ = ρ₂A₂V₂.
For incompressible flow this becomes A₁V₁ = A₂V₂ = Q (the volume flow rate). Halving the area doubles the speed.

Differential form
Applying the same balance to an infinitesimal element gives:
∂ρ/∂t + ∇·(ρV) = 0
For incompressible flow (ρ constant): ∇·V = ∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y + ∂w/∂z = 0.
This is a quick test of whether a proposed velocity field is physically possible. For example u = 2x, v = −2y gives ∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y = 2 − 2 = 0, so it satisfies continuity.

Worked example: Venturi meter
A Venturi meter carries water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³) from A₁ = 0.010 m² to a throat A₂ = 0.005 m², and the measured pressure difference is p₁ − p₂ = 2000 Pa.
- Continuity: V₁ = V₂(A₂/A₁) = 0.5V₂.
- Bernoulli: p₁ − p₂ = ½ρ(V₂² − V₁²) = ½ρV₂²(1 − 0.25).
- So V₂ = √(2 × 2000/(1000 × 0.75)) ≈ 2.31 m/s and Q = A₂V₂ ≈ 0.0115 m³/s (11.5 litres per second). In practice a discharge coefficient slightly below 1 corrects for losses.

Where mass conservation is used in aerodynamics
- Wind-tunnel contractions: area ratio sets the speed increase in the test section.
- Wake surveys: the mass flow deficit in the wake must be accounted for when choosing the control volume for a drag calculation.
- Boundary layers: the displacement thickness is defined using the mass flow deficit.
- Streamlines: in 2D incompressible flow, a stream function ψ with u = ∂ψ/∂y and v = −∂ψ/∂x satisfies continuity automatically; lines of constant ψ are streamlines, and the difference in ψ between two streamlines equals the volume flow per unit depth between them.

Exam tips: draw the control volume, mark inflows and outflows, and check that units of ṁ are kg/s. Always check continuity before using a given velocity field.

notes.h: Rotation of a fluid element: vorticity, circulation and irrotational flow
notes.body:
As a small fluid element moves, it can translate, rotate, stretch (linear strain) and shear (angular strain). Rotation matters because it decides whether Bernoulli holds across the whole flow and links directly to lift through circulation.

Angular velocity and vorticity
- In 2D, the angular velocity of an element about the z-axis is the average rotation rate of two initially perpendicular lines: ω_z = ½(∂v/∂x − ∂u/∂y).
- Vorticity is twice the angular velocity: ζ = ∇ × V. In 2D, ζ_z = ∂v/∂x − ∂u/∂y.
- A flow with ζ = 0 everywhere is irrotational.

Examples
- Solid-body rotation, u_θ = Ωr: every element rotates; vorticity = 2Ω everywhere.
- Free (potential) vortex, u_θ = Γ/(2πr): irrotational everywhere except at the centre, even though particles move in circles. Elements go round the centre without spinning about their own axes.
- Simple shear, u = ky, v = 0: ζ_z = −k, so it is rotational. Boundary layers are regions of vorticity for this reason.

Circulation
- Circulation is the line integral of velocity around a closed curve: Γ = ∮ V·dl.
- By Stokes' theorem, Γ equals the flux of vorticity through any surface bounded by the curve: Γ = ∬ ζ·n dA. So zero vorticity inside the curve means zero circulation, unless the region contains a singularity such as a vortex core or a body.
- Kelvin's circulation theorem: in inviscid flow of a barotropic fluid with conservative body forces, the circulation round a closed material curve stays constant. When an aerofoil starts moving, a starting vortex is shed so that the total circulation stays zero, leaving equal and opposite circulation bound to the aerofoil.

Irrotational (potential) flow
- If ∇ × V = 0, a velocity potential φ exists with V = ∇φ.
- Combined with incompressible continuity (∇·V = 0), this gives Laplace's equation ∇²φ = 0, which is linear, so elementary flows (uniform flow, source, sink, doublet, vortex) can be superposed to model flow round bodies.
- In irrotational flow, Bernoulli's constant is the same on every streamline, not just along one.

Why this matters
- Flow outside the thin boundary layer on a wing is close to irrotational, which is why potential-flow methods predict pressure distributions and lift well at small angles of attack.
- Lift needs circulation (Kutta–Joukowski), and circulation is the integrated vorticity in the boundary layer and wake.

Exam tips: calculate ω or ζ explicitly from the derivatives, keep track of signs, and remember that moving in a circle is not the same as rotating.

notes.h: Conservation of momentum: the control volume approach
notes.body:
Newton's second law applied to a control volume is the most useful tool in the module for finding forces from flow measurements: thrust, forces on pipe bends and nozzles, and drag from a wake survey.

Integral momentum equation
For a fixed control volume:
ΣF = d/dt ∫∫∫ ρV dV + ∯ ρV(V·n) dS
ΣF includes pressure forces on the CV surface, viscous forces, body forces such as gravity, and the force exerted by any solid object inside or cutting the CV.
For steady flow with uniform inlets and outlets:
ΣF = Σ(ṁV)_out − Σ(ṁV)_in
It is a vector equation, so apply it separately in x and y.

Procedure
- Draw the CV; mark inlets, outlets and every external force.
- Decide whether pressures are gauge or absolute (atmospheric pressure acting all round a CV cancels).
- Write mass conservation first, then momentum in each direction.
- Remember the force found is the force on the fluid; the force on the solid is equal and opposite.

Worked example 1: jet on a plate
A water jet of diameter 20 mm and speed 15 m/s hits a flat plate normal to it and spreads out sideways.
- A = π(0.01)² = 3.14 × 10⁻⁴ m², ṁ = 1000 × 3.14 × 10⁻⁴ × 15 = 4.71 kg/s.
- The outgoing flow has no component along the jet axis, so the force on the plate is F = ṁV = ρAV² ≈ 70.7 N.

Worked example 2: 90° pipe bend
Water at 0.05 m³/s flows through a horizontal 90° bend of diameter 150 mm with gauge pressure 150 kPa at inlet and outlet (losses ignored).
- A = 0.0177 m², V = 2.83 m/s, ṁ = 50 kg/s.
- Inlet flow in +x, outlet in +y. The force of the bend on the fluid: R_x = −(pA + ṁV) ≈ −2792 N and R_y = pA + ṁV ≈ +2792 N.
- The fluid pushes the bend with about 2.79 kN in +x and 2.79 kN in −y, a resultant of about 3.95 kN.

Drag from a wake survey
For a 2D body in a uniform stream, a CV whose upstream face is in undisturbed flow and whose downstream face cuts the wake (where pressure has returned to p∞) gives:
D′ = ρ ∫ u(U∞ − u) dy
taken across the wake. This accounts for mass leaving through the sides of the CV. It is how drag is measured with a Pitot rake behind an aerofoil.

Link to Bernoulli
Applying the momentum equation to a small element along a streamline with no viscosity gives Euler's equation, dp = −ρV dV for steady flow, which integrates to Bernoulli's equation for constant density.

Exam tips: most marks are lost on sign errors and missing pressure forces, so list every force explicitly, and state which way the force acts on which body.

Viscosity causes skin friction, pressure losses in pipes and the boundary layers that control separation and stall. Internal flow in pipes and channels is the simplest place to see its effects exactly.

Viscous stress and the no-slip condition
- At a solid wall, the fluid in contact has the same velocity as the wall (no slip).
- In a Newtonian fluid the shear stress is τ = μ du/dy. The wall shear stress τ_w = μ(du/dy) at the wall gives the skin friction.
- Skin friction coefficient: Cf = τ_w/(½ρU²).

Reynolds number and flow regime in a pipe
- Re_D = ρūD/μ, where ū is the mean velocity and D the diameter.
- Pipe flow is usually laminar below Re_D ≈ 2300; above that it can become turbulent (the exact transition depends on disturbances).

Fully developed laminar pipe flow (Hagen–Poiseuille)
A force balance on a cylinder of fluid gives τ = (r/2)(−dp/dx), leading to a parabolic profile:
- u(r) = (−dp/dx)(R² − r²)/(4μ)
- Centre-line velocity u_max = 2ū
- Volume flow Q = πR⁴(−dp/dx)/(8μ), i.e. Q = πR⁴Δp/(8μL)
Note the R⁴ dependence: halving the radius cuts the flow by a factor of 16 at the same pressure gradient.

Pressure loss and friction factor
- Darcy–Weisbach: Δp = f (L/D) ½ρū².
- For laminar flow f = 64/Re_D (this follows directly from Hagen–Poiseuille).
- For turbulent flow, f depends on Re_D and relative roughness and is read from the Moody chart or a correlation such as Colebrook's.

Worked example
Water (μ = 1.0 × 10⁻³ Pa s) flows in a 10 mm pipe at ū = 0.1 m/s.
- Re_D = 1000 × 0.1 × 0.01/0.001 = 1000, so laminar.
- f = 64/1000 = 0.064, so Δp/L = 0.064 × (1/0.01) × ½ × 1000 × 0.1² = 32 Pa/m.
- Check with Hagen–Poiseuille: Δp/L = 32μū/D² = 32 × 0.001 × 0.1/0.0001 = 32 Pa/m.

Entrance region
- Near a pipe inlet, a boundary layer grows from the wall until it fills the pipe; after that the flow is fully developed.
- Laminar entrance length is roughly L_e ≈ 0.06 Re_D D (about 0.6 m in the example above). Turbulent entrance lengths are much shorter relative to Re.

Couette flow
Fluid between a fixed plate and a plate moving at speed U, with no pressure gradient, has a linear profile u = Uy/h and uniform shear stress τ = μU/h. This models lubrication films.

Exam tips: always find Re first to decide laminar or turbulent; quote f = 64/Re only for laminar flow, and keep Darcy (64/Re) and Fanning (16/Re) friction factors distinct.

notes.h: Boundary layers, turbulence and finite wings
notes.body:
The last part of the module joins viscous flow to real wings: boundary layers, transition to turbulence, separation, and the three-dimensional effects that give induced drag.

Boundary layers
- A thin layer next to a surface where viscosity slows the flow from the outer velocity U to zero at the wall.
- Thickness δ (often δ₉₉, where u = 0.99U).
- Displacement thickness δ* = ∫(1 − u/U) dy: how far the outer flow is pushed away by the mass-flow deficit.
- Momentum thickness θ = ∫(u/U)(1 − u/U) dy: related to the momentum deficit, and so to skin-friction drag.

Laminar flat plate (Blasius) results, with Re_x = Ux/ν:
- δ ≈ 5.0x/√Re_x
- Local Cf = 0.664/√Re_x; average over length L, CF = 1.328/√Re_L (one side).
Example: U = 10 m/s, x = 0.3 m, ν = 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s gives Re_x = 2 × 10⁵, δ ≈ 3.4 mm and local Cf ≈ 0.0015.

Transition and turbulence
- On a smooth flat plate, transition typically starts around Re_x ≈ 5 × 10⁵ (approximately; it depends strongly on freestream turbulence and roughness).
- Turbulent flow is unsteady, three-dimensional, rotational and strongly mixing. Velocity is split into mean and fluctuation (Reynolds decomposition): u = ū + u′.
- Turbulent boundary layers are thicker (a common approximation is δ ≈ 0.37x/Re_x^(1/5)), have fuller velocity profiles and higher wall shear, so more skin friction, but they resist separation better.

Separation
- An adverse pressure gradient (pressure rising in the flow direction) slows the near-wall fluid. When the wall shear falls to zero, the flow separates.
- Separation causes stall on wings and large pressure drag on bluff bodies. Turbulent layers, with more momentum near the wall, separate later: this is why golf balls are dimpled.

Finite wings
- Aspect ratio AR = b²/S (b = span, S = wing area).
- High pressure below and low pressure above drive flow round the wingtips, forming trailing (tip) vortices.
- These induce a downwash at the wing, tilting the local flow and the lift vector backwards. The rearward component is induced drag.
- Induced drag coefficient: CDi = CL²/(πeAR), where e is the span efficiency factor (e = 1 for an elliptical lift distribution).
- The 3D lift-curve slope is lower than the 2D value: approximately a = a₀/(1 + a₀/(πeAR)).

Worked example: AR = 8, e = 1, CL = 0.5
- CDi = 0.25/(π × 8) ≈ 0.0099
- With a₀ = 2π per rad, a = 2π/(1 + 2/8) ≈ 5.03 per rad (about 0.088 per degree) compared with about 0.110 per degree in 2D.
Induced drag matters most at low speed and high CL (take-off, climb), which is why gliders use high aspect ratios.

Exam tips: state whether a result is laminar or turbulent, and in induced-drag questions check that e and AR are used correctly and that CDi scales with CL².

cards.b: A substance that deforms continuously under any applied shear stress, however small; it cannot resist shear by a fixed deformation as a solid does.
Treating the fluid as continuous so properties vary smoothly with position; valid when flow length scales are much larger than the molecular mean free path.
τ = μ du/dy: shear stress is proportional to the velocity gradient normal to the flow; μ is the dynamic viscosity.
Streamline: tangent to velocity at an instant. Pathline: path of one particle. Streakline: particles that passed one point. All coincide in steady flow.
Steady, inviscid, incompressible flow along a streamline with no work or heat added (or anywhere in an irrotational flow).
q = ½ρV². Total (stagnation) pressure p₀ = p + ½ρV² in incompressible flow.

cards.f: When can air be treated as incompressible?
cards.b: Approximately when M < 0.3, where density changes are under about 5%.
The angle between the aerofoil chord line and the oncoming freestream velocity.
Maximum distance between the mean camber line and the chord line, usually as a % of chord. Zero for a symmetric aerofoil.
Cp = (p − p∞)/(½ρ∞V∞²). In incompressible inviscid flow Cp = 1 − (V/V∞)²; Cp = 1 at a stagnation point.
Lift is perpendicular to the freestream; drag is parallel to it. They are not defined relative to the chord line.
Flow leaves a sharp trailing edge smoothly with finite velocity; this sets the circulation, and hence the lift, around the aerofoil.
Lift per unit span L′ = ρ∞V∞Γ, where Γ is the circulation around the aerofoil.
dCl/dα = 2π per radian (≈ 0.11 per degree), an approximate result for thin aerofoils at small α.
Loss of lift at high angle of attack when the boundary layer separates from the upper surface; drag also rises sharply.
6.5 K per km (T = 288.15 − 0.0065h) from sea level to 11 km.
Constant at 216.65 K (−56.5 °C): the lower stratosphere is isothermal in the ISA.
dp/dh = −ρg: pressure falls with height because each layer supports the weight of the air above it.
p/p₀ = (T/T₀)^(g/(λR)) with g/(λR) ≈ 5.256 for air.
a = √(γRT); about 340 m/s at 288 K and about 295 m/s at 216.65 K.
The ISA altitude that has the same density as the actual air. Hot, high conditions give a high density altitude and poorer performance.
Total (stagnation) pressure p₀, because the flow is brought to rest at its open end facing the flow.
A small, burr-free hole drilled normal to a surface; it senses local static pressure.
V = √(2(p₀ − p)/ρ) for incompressible flow, using the local air density.
Δp = ρ_liquid g h, using the density of the manometer liquid, not the air.
EAS = TAS × √σ, where σ = ρ/ρ₀. It is the sea-level speed giving the same dynamic pressure.
Heated fine wire; heat loss (hence voltage) depends on velocity. High frequency response, so used for turbulence. Needs calibration; fragile.
Seeded flow lit by a pulsed laser sheet; cross-correlating paired images gives the velocity field over a plane.
A problem with n variables and k independent base dimensions can be expressed with n − k independent dimensionless groups.
Re = ρVL/μ = VL/ν: ratio of inertial to viscous forces.
M = V/a: ratio of flow speed to speed of sound; governs compressibility effects.
[M L⁻¹ T⁻¹] (units Pa s or kg/(m s)).

Pick k variables that together contain all base dimensions but cannot form a dimensionless group themselves (e.g. ρ, V, L).

cards.f: Ways to raise Re in a wind tunnel
cards.b: Increase density (pressurised tunnel), lower viscosity and raise density (cryogenic tunnel), or test in water.
ṁ = ρAV for uniform flow normal to area A (kg/s).

cards.b: A₁V₁ = A₂V₂ = Q: smaller area means higher velocity.
∂ρ/∂t + ∇·(ρV) = 0; for incompressible flow ∇·V = 0.
d/dt ∫ρ dV + ∯ρ(V·n) dS = 0: rate of mass increase inside + net outflow through the surface = 0.
u = ∂ψ/∂y, v = −∂ψ/∂x; continuity is satisfied automatically and ψ is constant along streamlines.
Continuity relates throat and inlet speeds; Bernoulli links the speed change to the measured pressure drop, giving the flow rate.

cards.f: 2D angular velocity of a fluid element

cards.b: ζ = ∇ × V, equal to twice the local angular velocity of a fluid element.
A flow with zero vorticity everywhere; then a velocity potential φ exists with V = ∇φ.
Γ = ∮V·dl around a closed curve; by Stokes' theorem it equals the vorticity flux through the enclosed surface.

cards.b: 2Ω everywhere (every element spins at Ω).
Irrotational everywhere except at r = 0; particles circle the centre without spinning.
In inviscid, barotropic flow with conservative body forces, circulation round a closed material curve is constant in time.
Incompressible + irrotational flow gives ∇²φ = 0, which is linear so elementary flows can be superposed.
ΣF = Σ(ṁV)_out − Σ(ṁV)_in (vector equation), with ΣF including pressure, body and solid-surface forces on the fluid.

cards.f: Force of a jet hitting a normal flat plate
cards.b: F = ṁV = ρAV², when the jet leaves the plate with no velocity component along its original axis.
D′ = ρ∫u(U∞ − u) dy across the wake, taken where the wake pressure has returned to freestream.

cards.f: Why use gauge pressures on a CV?
cards.b: Atmospheric pressure acting all round a closed surface gives zero net force, so it can be removed by using gauge pressures.
dp = −ρV dV; integrating at constant density gives Bernoulli's equation.

cards.f: Force on fluid vs force on solid
cards.b: The momentum equation gives the force on the fluid; by Newton's third law the force on the solid is equal and opposite.
Fluid in contact with a solid surface has the same velocity as the surface.
Re_D ≈ 2300 (approximately); below this pipe flow is normally laminar.
Q = πR⁴Δp/(8μL) for fully developed laminar pipe flow.
Parabolic: u(r) = (−dp/dx)(R² − r²)/(4μ); u_max = 2ū.
Δp = f(L/D)(½ρū²); laminar Darcy friction factor f = 64/Re_D.
Approximately L_e ≈ 0.06 Re_D D before the flow is fully developed.
Flow between a fixed and a moving plate with no pressure gradient: linear profile u = Uy/h, uniform τ = μU/h.
δ* = ∫(1 − u/U)dy: the distance the outer flow is displaced by the boundary layer's mass-flow deficit.
θ = ∫(u/U)(1 − u/U)dy: measures the momentum deficit in the boundary layer; linked to skin-friction drag.
δ ≈ 5.0x/√Re_x on a flat plate with zero pressure gradient.
Roughly Re_x ≈ 5 × 10⁵, though it varies with freestream turbulence and surface roughness.
Flow detaches when an adverse pressure gradient reduces wall shear to zero; causes stall and pressure drag.
AR = b²/S (span squared over wing area); equals b/c for a rectangular wing.
CDi = CL²/(πeAR); e = 1 for an elliptical lift distribution.
Turbulent mixing brings high-momentum fluid towards the wall, so the near-wall flow can push further against an adverse pressure gradient.

questions.q: Which set of assumptions is required to apply Bernoulli's equation p + ½ρV² = constant along a streamline?
options: Steady, inviscid, incompressible flow with no work added
Steady, viscous flow with a fan adding energy
Any flow, provided the fluid is a gas
questions.why: Bernoulli's equation comes from integrating Euler's (inviscid) momentum equation along a streamline for steady, constant-density flow with no shaft work. Viscous or unsteady compressible flow breaks the derivation; a fan adds energy, so the total pressure is not constant through it; and being a gas does not make the equation valid on its own.

questions.q: Air (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³) speeds up from 20 m/s to 40 m/s along a streamline in steady, inviscid, incompressible flow. What is the change in static pressure?
questions.why: Δp = −½ρ(V₂² − V₁²) = −0.5 × 1.225 × (1600 − 400) = −735 Pa, so pressure falls by 735 Pa. A rise of 735 Pa has the wrong sign (faster flow means lower static pressure). 245 Pa comes from using (40 − 20)² instead of the difference of the squares, and 980 Pa is ½ρV² at 40 m/s alone, ignoring the initial speed.

questions.q: State the continuum hypothesis and explain why it lets us use calculus to describe a flow. Give one situation where it would break down.
markScheme: Defines the hypothesis: fluid treated as continuous; properties defined at every point
Validity condition: flow length scale ≫ molecular mean free path (Knudsen number small)
Consequence: ρ, p, V become smooth fields so derivatives/differential equations can be used
Valid breakdown example, e.g. very rarefied gas at high altitude or micro-scale flow
questions.modelAnswer: The continuum hypothesis treats a fluid as a continuous medium rather than a collection of molecules, so properties such as density, pressure and velocity have a definite value at every point and vary smoothly. This is justified when the length scale of the flow (a wing chord, a pipe diameter) is far larger than the molecular mean free path, i.e. the Knudsen number is small. Because the properties are smooth fields, we can take derivatives and write conservation laws as differential equations. It breaks down in very rarefied gas, for example a spacecraft at the edge of the atmosphere, or in flow through passages only a few mean free paths wide.

questions.q: At the stagnation point on an aerofoil in low-speed (incompressible) flow, what is the pressure coefficient?
options: It depends on the angle of attack
questions.why: At a stagnation point V = 0, so Cp = 1 − (0/V∞)² = 1, which is the maximum Cp in incompressible flow. Cp = 0 would mean the local pressure equals freestream pressure (local speed equals V∞). Cp = −1 corresponds to a local speed of √2 V∞, not zero speed. The stagnation point moves with angle of attack, but its Cp is still 1.

questions.q: A thin symmetric aerofoil is at 4° angle of attack. Using thin aerofoil theory, roughly what lift coefficient is expected?
questions.why: Cl = 2πα with α in radians: 2π × (4π/180) = 0.439, so about 0.44. A value of about 25 comes from multiplying 2π by 4 degrees without converting to radians. 0.11 is the slope per degree, not the lift at 4°. A symmetric aerofoil has zero lift only at zero angle of attack.

questions.q: Explain how a sharp trailing edge leads to lift on an aerofoil, referring to the Kutta condition and the Kutta–Joukowski theorem. Calculate the lift per unit span when ρ = 1.225 kg/m³, V∞ = 50 m/s and Γ = 20 m²/s.
markScheme: Without circulation, inviscid flow would wrap around the sharp trailing edge with infinite velocity
Kutta condition: flow leaves the trailing edge smoothly, which fixes a unique circulation Γ
Kutta–Joukowski: L′ = ρ∞V∞Γ, so lift is proportional to circulation
Calculation: L′ = 1.225 × 50 × 20 = 1225 N/m
Notes that viscosity (the starting vortex/boundary layer) is what establishes the Kutta condition in reality
questions.modelAnswer: In inviscid potential flow around an aerofoil with no circulation, the flow would have to turn sharply around the trailing edge, giving infinite velocity there. Real flow does not do this; viscous effects make it leave the sharp trailing edge smoothly. This is the Kutta condition, and it picks out one particular value of the circulation Γ around the section (as the flow starts, a starting vortex is shed so that the total circulation is conserved). The Kutta–Joukowski theorem then gives the lift per unit span as L′ = ρ∞V∞Γ. Here L′ = 1.225 × 50 × 20 = 1225 N/m.

questions.q: In the ISA, which statement about the layer from 11 km to 20 km is correct?
options: Temperature is constant at 216.65 K and pressure falls exponentially with height
Temperature falls at 6.5 K/km and pressure falls exponentially
Temperature rises at 6.5 K/km and pressure is constant
Temperature and pressure are both constant
questions.why: From 11 to 20 km the ISA is isothermal at 216.65 K, and integrating dp/p = −g dh/(RT) with constant T gives an exponential pressure decay. The 6.5 K/km lapse rate applies to the troposphere below 11 km, where the pressure law is a power law rather than exponential. Pressure can never be constant with height, because hydrostatic balance requires it to fall.

questions.q: Using the ISA, what is the approximate air density at 5000 m?
questions.why: T = 255.65 K and p ≈ 54.0 kPa, so ρ = p/(RT) ≈ 0.736 kg/m³. 1.23 kg/m³ is the sea-level value, so it ignores the fall in density with height. 0.41 kg/m³ is roughly the density at 10 km, not 5 km. 0.65 kg/m³ comes from dividing the 5 km pressure by the sea-level temperature (54 020/(287.05 × 288.15)) instead of the local temperature of 255.65 K.

questions.q: Starting from the hydrostatic equation and the ideal gas law, derive the expression for pressure in the ISA troposphere, and evaluate the pressure at 3000 m.
markScheme: dp/dh = −ρg and p = ρRT combined to dp/p = −g dh/(RT)
Substitutes T = T₀ − λh so dh = −dT/λ, giving dp/p = (g/(λR)) dT/T
Integrates to p/p₀ = (T/T₀)^(g/(λR)), exponent ≈ 5.26
p ≈ 70.1 kPa
questions.modelAnswer: Hydrostatic balance gives dp/dh = −ρg, and the ideal gas law gives ρ = p/(RT). Dividing, dp/p = −g dh/(RT). In the troposphere T = T₀ − λh, so dT = −λ dh and dh = −dT/λ. Then dp/p = (g/(λR)) dT/T. Integrating from sea level: ln(p/p₀) = (g/(λR)) ln(T/T₀), so p/p₀ = (T/T₀)^(g/(λR)). With g = 9.81, λ = 0.0065 K/m and R = 287.05, the exponent is about 5.258 (5.256 with the standard g = 9.80665). At 3000 m, T = 288.15 − 19.5 = 268.65 K, so p = 101 325 × (268.65/288.15)^5.258 ≈ 70 100 Pa (about 70.1 kPa).

questions.q: A Pitot-static tube in a sea-level wind tunnel is connected to a water manometer that reads 30 mm. What is the airspeed (take ρ_water = 1000 kg/m³, ρ_air = 1.225 kg/m³)?
questions.why: Δp = 1000 × 9.81 × 0.03 = 294.3 Pa, and V = √(2 × 294.3/1.225) ≈ 21.9 m/s. About 0.77 m/s comes from using the water density in the velocity formula as well. About 480 m/s is 2Δp/ρ_air without the square root. About 7.0 m/s comes from treating the 30 mm reading as if it were 30 Pa instead of converting it with Δp = ρ_water g h.

questions.q: Which instrument is best suited to measuring rapid velocity fluctuations at a point in a turbulent boundary layer?
options: Pitot tube with a water manometer
questions.why: A hot-wire anemometer has a very small, fast-responding sensor, so it can follow turbulent fluctuations at high frequency. A Pitot tube with a liquid manometer responds far too slowly and gives only time-averaged pressure. Oil flow shows surface flow patterns, not velocity. Smoke photographs show flow structure qualitatively but do not give quantitative point velocity time histories.

questions.q: An aircraft flies at 3000 m in the ISA (ρ ≈ 0.909 kg/m³). Its Pitot-static system measures p₀ − p = 1500 Pa. Find the true airspeed and the equivalent airspeed, and explain the difference.
markScheme: EAS uses sea-level density; TAS uses local density
EAS = TAS√σ; EAS < TAS at altitude because σ < 1
questions.modelAnswer: The true airspeed uses the local density: TAS = √(2 × 1500/0.909) ≈ 57.4 m/s. The equivalent airspeed uses sea-level density: EAS = √(2 × 1500/1.225) ≈ 49.5 m/s. Both give the same dynamic pressure, which is what governs aerodynamic forces, so EAS is the speed that would give the same forces at sea level. Since EAS = TAS√σ and σ ≈ 0.742 at 3000 m, EAS is lower than TAS at altitude.

questions.q: Drag F on a sphere depends on ρ, V, diameter D and μ. How many independent dimensionless groups describe the problem?
questions.why: There are 5 variables (F, ρ, V, D, μ) and 3 base dimensions (M, L, T), so the Π theorem gives 5 − 3 = 2 groups: a drag coefficient and the Reynolds number. 3 would need an extra variable such as the speed of sound. 4 subtracts only one dimension, and 5 is just the number of variables.

questions.q: A 1/5-scale model is tested in the same air as the full-size aircraft. To match the full-scale Reynolds number, the model airspeed must be:
options: The same as the full-scale speed
questions.why: With ρ and μ unchanged, Re = ρVL/μ is matched only if VL is the same, so a model one-fifth the size needs five times the speed. One-fifth of the speed would make Re 25 times too small. The same speed would make Re five times too small. √5 times the speed has no basis in Reynolds-number matching (it gives Re only √5/5 ≈ 0.45 of full scale); Froude matching, which keeps V/√(gL) equal, would actually call for 1/√5 of the full-scale speed, not √5 times.

questions.q: The power P needed to drive a propeller depends on fluid density ρ, rotational speed n (rev/s), diameter D and forward speed V. Use dimensional analysis with ρ, n and D as repeating variables to find the dimensionless groups.
markScheme: Lists dimensions: P [ML²T⁻³], ρ [ML⁻³], n [T⁻¹], D [L], V [LT⁻¹]
n = 5, k = 3 so 2 groups
Π₁ = P/(ρn³D⁵) (power coefficient), with exponent working shown
Π₂ = V/(nD) (advance ratio)
Final relation P/(ρn³D⁵) = f(V/(nD))
questions.modelAnswer: Dimensions: P is [ML²T⁻³], ρ [ML⁻³], n [T⁻¹], D [L] and V [LT⁻¹]. With 5 variables and 3 dimensions there are 2 groups. For power, try Π₁ = P ρᵃ nᵇ Dᶜ. Mass: 1 + a = 0 so a = −1. Time: −3 − b = 0 so b = −3. Length: 2 − 3a + c = 0 so c = −5. Hence Π₁ = P/(ρn³D⁵), the power coefficient. For velocity, Π₂ = V ρᵃ nᵇ Dᶜ: mass gives a = 0, time gives −1 − b = 0 so b = −1, length gives 1 + c = 0 so c = −1, so Π₂ = V/(nD), the advance ratio. Therefore P/(ρn³D⁵) = f(V/(nD)). (Viscosity and compressibility have been neglected.)

questions.q: Which of these 2D velocity fields satisfies incompressible continuity?
questions.why: Incompressible continuity requires ∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y = 0. For u = 3x, v = −3y this is 3 − 3 = 0. For u = 3x, v = 3y it is 6. For u = x², v = y² it is 2x + 2y, not zero everywhere. For u = 3y, v = 3y it is 0 + 3 = 3.

questions.q: Water flows steadily through a pipe that narrows from 100 mm diameter to 50 mm diameter. If the speed in the wide section is 1 m/s, what is the speed in the narrow section?
questions.why: A₁V₁ = A₂V₂ and area scales with diameter squared, so V₂ = 1 × (100/50)² = 4 m/s. 2 m/s scales with diameter instead of area. 0.25 m/s inverts the ratio, and 1 m/s ignores the change in area.

questions.q: A Venturi meter carries water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³). The inlet area is 0.010 m² and the throat area 0.005 m². The pressure difference between inlet and throat is 2000 Pa. Assuming ideal flow, find the volume flow rate.
markScheme: Continuity: V₁ = (A₂/A₁)V₂ = 0.5V₂
Bernoulli: p₁ − p₂ = ½ρ(V₂² − V₁²)
Combines: V₂ = √(2Δp/(ρ(1 − (A₂/A₁)²))) ≈ 2.31 m/s
Q = A₂V₂ ≈ 0.0115 m³/s
States ideal-flow assumptions (inviscid, steady, incompressible, horizontal)
questions.modelAnswer: Assume steady, inviscid, incompressible flow in a horizontal meter. Continuity gives V₁ = (A₂/A₁)V₂ = 0.5V₂. Bernoulli between inlet and throat gives p₁ − p₂ = ½ρ(V₂² − V₁²) = ½ρV₂²(1 − 0.25). So V₂ = √(2 × 2000/(1000 × 0.75)) = √5.33 ≈ 2.31 m/s. The flow rate is Q = A₂V₂ = 0.005 × 2.31 ≈ 0.0115 m³/s, about 11.5 litres per second.

questions.q: For the 2D flow u = 4y, v = 0, what is the vorticity ζ_z?
questions.why: ζ_z = ∂v/∂x − ∂u/∂y = 0 − 4 = −4. Plus 4 has the sign reversed. −2 is the angular velocity ω_z (half the vorticity), not the vorticity. Zero would be correct only if the flow were irrotational, but a shear flow like this is rotational.

questions.q: Which statement about a free (potential) vortex u_θ = Γ/(2πr) is correct?
options: Fluid particles move in circles but the flow is irrotational away from the centre
The flow has uniform vorticity equal to 2Γ
The flow rotates like a solid body
The circulation round any closed curve is zero
questions.why: In a free vortex the vorticity is zero for r > 0, so elements circle the centre without spinning. Uniform vorticity describes solid-body rotation, not a free vortex, and 2Γ is not even dimensionally a vorticity. Solid-body rotation has u_θ proportional to r, not 1/r. The circulation round a curve enclosing the centre equals Γ, not zero; it is zero only for curves that do not enclose the centre.

questions.q: A 2D flow is given by u = x − y, v = x + y. Show whether it is (a) incompressible and (b) irrotational. Comment on whether the incompressible Bernoulli equation can be applied between any two points in the flow.
markScheme: ∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y = 1 + 1 = 2 ≠ 0, so it is not incompressible
ζ_z = ∂v/∂x − ∂u/∂y = 1 − (−1) = 2 ≠ 0, so it is rotational
Correct use of definitions with signs
Bernoulli between arbitrary points needs irrotational (and incompressible) flow, so it cannot be applied across streamlines here
questions.modelAnswer: (a) ∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y = 1 + 1 = 2, which is not zero, so the field does not satisfy incompressible continuity; it could only describe a flow with changing density. (b) ζ_z = ∂v/∂x − ∂u/∂y = 1 − (−1) = 2, so the flow is rotational, with angular velocity 1 rad/s. Bernoulli with the same constant everywhere requires steady, inviscid, incompressible, irrotational flow. This flow is neither incompressible nor irrotational, so the incompressible Bernoulli equation cannot be applied between arbitrary points.

questions.q: A water jet of area 3.14 × 10⁻⁴ m² and speed 15 m/s strikes a flat plate normally and spreads radially. What is the force on the plate?
questions.why: F = ρAV² = 1000 × 3.14 × 10⁻⁴ × 225 ≈ 70.7 N. About 4.7 N is the mass flow rate in kg/s, not a force. About 35.3 N wrongly includes a factor of ½ as if it were a dynamic pressure force. About 141 N doubles the answer, which would apply only if the jet were turned back through 180°.

questions.q: In a wake survey behind a 2D aerofoil, why is the drag D′ = ρ∫u(U∞ − u)dy rather than ρ∫(U∞² − u²)dy?
options: The wake has a mass-flow deficit, so some fluid must leave through the sides of the control volume carrying momentum U∞
The pressure in the wake is always higher than freestream
Viscous stresses on the downstream face are large
The formula with U∞² − u² applies only to compressible flow
questions.why: Because u < U∞ in the wake, less mass leaves through the downstream face than enters upstream; the difference leaves through the side boundaries with velocity about U∞. Including that momentum flux gives ρ∫u(U∞ − u)dy. The survey is taken where wake pressure has returned to freestream, not where it is higher. Viscous stresses on a face normal to the flow far downstream are negligible. The U∞² − u² form is not a compressible-flow result; it is simply the wrong result because it ignores the side outflow.

questions.q: Water flows at 0.05 m³/s through a horizontal 90° pipe bend of internal diameter 150 mm. The gauge pressure is 150 kPa at both inlet and outlet. The flow enters in the +x direction and leaves in the +y direction. Find the magnitude and direction of the force exerted by the water on the bend.
markScheme: x-momentum: p₁A + R_x = ṁ(0 − V) so R_x ≈ −2792 N
y-momentum: −p₂A + R_y = ṁ(V − 0) so R_y ≈ +2792 N
Force on bend = −R: about 2.79 kN in +x and 2.79 kN in −y
Resultant ≈ 3.95 kN at 45° below the +x axis
questions.modelAnswer: A = π(0.15)²/4 = 0.01767 m², V = Q/A = 2.83 m/s, ṁ = ρQ = 50 kg/s. Let R be the force of the bend on the water. In x, the inlet pressure force p₁A = 2651 N acts in +x, and the x-momentum goes from ṁV to zero: 2651 + R_x = 50 × (0 − 2.83), so R_x ≈ −2792 N. In y, the outlet pressure force acts in −y (it pushes back into the CV), and y-momentum goes from zero to ṁV: −2651 + R_y = 50 × 2.83, so R_y ≈ +2792 N. The force of the water on the bend is −R, which is about 2792 N in +x and 2792 N in −y: a resultant of √2 × 2792 ≈ 3950 N acting at 45° below the +x direction (pushing the bend outwards, away from the corner).

questions.q: In fully developed laminar flow in a pipe, how does the volume flow rate change if the radius is halved but the pressure gradient is kept constant?
options: It falls to 1/16 of its original value
questions.why: Hagen–Poiseuille gives Q ∝ R⁴ at fixed pressure gradient, so halving R gives (1/2)⁴ = 1/16. A quarter would follow if Q scaled with area only (fixed mean velocity). A half would be a linear dependence on radius. The flow cannot be unchanged because both the area and the mean velocity fall.

questions.q: Water (μ = 0.001 Pa s, ρ = 1000 kg/m³) flows at a mean speed of 0.5 m/s in a 50 mm pipe. Which description fits best?
options: Re ≈ 25 000, so the flow is likely turbulent
Re ≈ 25, so the flow is laminar
Re ≈ 2500, so the flow is definitely laminar
Re ≈ 250 000, so the flow is laminar because water is viscous
questions.why: Re = 1000 × 0.5 × 0.05/0.001 = 25 000, well above about 2300, so turbulent flow is expected. Re ≈ 25 and Re ≈ 250 000 come from unit slips by factors of 1000 and 10. Re ≈ 2500 is also a factor-of-ten error, and even that value would sit near transition rather than being definitely laminar.

questions.q: Water (μ = 1.0 × 10⁻³ Pa s, ρ = 1000 kg/m³) flows at mean speed 0.1 m/s in a 10 mm diameter pipe. Show the flow is laminar, find the pressure drop over 5 m of pipe, and state the centre-line velocity.
markScheme: Re_D = 1000, below about 2300, so laminar
Cross-check 32μūL/D² = 160 Pa
u_max = 2ū = 0.2 m/s
questions.modelAnswer: Re_D = ρūD/μ = 1000 × 0.1 × 0.01/0.001 = 1000, which is below about 2300, so the flow is laminar. The Darcy friction factor is f = 64/Re = 0.064. Then Δp = f(L/D)(½ρū²) = 0.064 × (5/0.01) × (0.5 × 1000 × 0.01) = 0.064 × 500 × 5 = 160 Pa. As a check, Hagen–Poiseuille gives Δp = 32μūL/D² = 32 × 0.001 × 0.1 × 5/0.0001 = 160 Pa. For a parabolic profile the centre-line velocity is twice the mean: 0.2 m/s.

questions.q: A wing with aspect ratio 8 and span efficiency 1 flies at CL = 0.5. What is the induced drag coefficient?
questions.why: CDi = CL²/(πeAR) = 0.25/(π × 8) ≈ 0.0099. About 0.020 uses CL instead of CL², giving 0.5/(8π). About 0.031 divides CL² by AR but leaves out π (0.25/8). About 0.0625 divides CL² by 4, which has no basis in the formula.

questions.q: Why does a turbulent boundary layer usually separate later than a laminar one on the same surface?
options: Turbulent mixing transfers high-momentum fluid towards the wall
It is thinner than a laminar layer
Turbulence removes the adverse pressure gradient
questions.why: Turbulent mixing carries faster fluid from the outer layer down to the wall, so the near-wall flow has more momentum to overcome an adverse pressure gradient. Turbulent layers actually have higher skin friction and are thicker than laminar ones at the same Re_x. The pressure gradient is set by the outer flow and body shape; turbulence does not remove it.

questions.q: Explain why a finite wing has induced drag and why it has a lower lift-curve slope than its aerofoil section. Calculate the 3D lift-curve slope for a wing of aspect ratio 6 with e = 0.9 and a₀ = 2π per radian.
markScheme: Pressure difference drives flow round the tips, forming trailing vortices
Vortices induce downwash, reducing the effective angle of attack
Lift vector tilts back; its rearward component is induced drag, CDi = CL²/(πeAR)
Reduced effective α means less lift per unit geometric α, so lower slope
questions.modelAnswer: On a finite wing, high pressure under the wing and low pressure above drive air round the wingtips, producing trailing vortices. These induce a downwash over the wing, so the local flow arrives at a smaller effective angle of attack than the geometric angle. The lift, which is perpendicular to the local flow, is tilted backwards, and its component along the freestream is the induced drag, CDi = CL²/(πeAR). Because the effective angle of attack is reduced, the wing produces less lift per degree than the 2D section, so its lift-curve slope is lower. With a₀ = 2π, e = 0.9 and AR = 6: a = 2π/(1 + 2π/(π × 0.9 × 6)) = 2π/(1 + 0.370) ≈ 4.59 per radian (about 0.080 per degree).

questions.q: An aircraft cruises at 5000 m in the International Standard Atmosphere. Its Pitot-static system records p₀ − p = 4000 Pa. (a) Starting from the hydrostatic equation and ideal gas law, derive the ISA troposphere relations for p/p₀ and ρ/ρ₀. [7] (b) Find the temperature, pressure, density and speed of sound at 5000 m. [5] (c) Find the true airspeed, the equivalent airspeed and the Mach number. [5] (d) Comment on whether the incompressible Pitot formula is adequate here, and on one other source of error. [3] Take T₀ = 288.15 K, p₀ = 101 325 Pa, ρ₀ = 1.225 kg/m³, λ = 6.5 K/km, R = 287.05 J/(kg K), γ = 1.4, g = 9.81 m/s².
markScheme: (a) dp/dh = −ρg with ρ = p/(RT) gives dp/p = −g dh/(RT)
(a) With T = T₀ − λh, integrates to p/p₀ = (T/T₀)^(g/(λR)), exponent ≈ 5.26; ρ/ρ₀ = (T/T₀)^(g/(λR) − 1)
(d) M ≈ 0.33 is just above 0.3, so compressibility error is small (of order M²/4 ≈ 3% in Δp) but not zero
(d) Other error: static port position error, probe misalignment, instrument lag or calibration
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Hydrostatic balance on a thin horizontal slab gives dp/dh = −ρg. Substituting ρ = p/(RT): dp/p = −g dh/(RT). In the troposphere T = T₀ − λh, so dh = −dT/λ and dp/p = (g/(λR)) dT/T. Integrating from sea level gives ln(p/p₀) = (g/(λR)) ln(T/T₀), so
p/p₀ = (T/T₀)^(g/(λR)), with g/(λR) = 9.81/(0.0065 × 287.05) ≈ 5.258 (5.256 if the standard g = 9.80665 is used).
Dividing by the ideal gas law ρ/ρ₀ = (p/p₀)(T₀/T) gives ρ/ρ₀ = (T/T₀)^(g/(λR) − 1) = (T/T₀)^4.258.

(b) T = 288.15 − 0.0065 × 5000 = 255.65 K.
T/T₀ = 0.8872, so p = 101 325 × 0.8872^5.258 ≈ 54 010 Pa (54.0 kPa).
ρ = p/(RT) = 54 010/(287.05 × 255.65) ≈ 0.736 kg/m³ (σ ≈ 0.601).
a = √(1.4 × 287.05 × 255.65) ≈ 320.5 m/s.

(c) Incompressible Pitot formula with local density: TAS = √(2 × 4000/0.736) ≈ 104 m/s.
Equivalent airspeed uses sea-level density: EAS = √(2 × 4000/1.225) ≈ 80.8 m/s (check: TAS√σ = 104.3 × 0.775 ≈ 80.8 m/s).
Mach number M = 104.3/320.5 ≈ 0.33.

(d) The incompressible formula assumes density does not change as the flow stagnates in the probe. At M ≈ 0.33 the flow is just above the usual M = 0.3 guideline; the compressible correction to the measured pressure difference is of order M²/4, about 3%, so the incompressible result slightly overestimates the speed but is acceptable for a first estimate. Other errors include static-port position error (the local static pressure on the fuselage differs from freestream), Pitot misalignment at high angle of attack, and instrument lag or calibration error.

questions.q: A 2D aerofoil of chord 0.20 m is tested in a wind tunnel at U∞ = 30 m/s, ρ = 1.225 kg/m³. A Pitot rake far downstream, where the static pressure has returned to p∞, shows a symmetric triangular wake: u(y) = U∞[1 − 0.15(1 − |y|/h)] for |y| ≤ h with h = 0.02 m, and u = U∞ outside. (a) Using a control volume, derive D′ = ρ∫u(U∞ − u)dy, explaining the role of mass conservation. [8] (b) Calculate the mass-flow deficit per unit span in the wake. [3] (c) Calculate D′ and the section drag coefficient Cd. [6] (d) State two assumptions and one practical limitation of the method. [3]
markScheme: (a) CV with upstream face in uniform flow, downstream face across wake, sides parallel to freestream
(a) Mass: side outflow = ρ∫(U∞ − u)dy, leaving with x-velocity ≈ U∞
(a) x-momentum: −D′ = ρ∫u²dy + U∞ρ∫(U∞ − u)dy − ρ∫U∞²dy, giving D′ = ρ∫u(U∞ − u)dy
(b) Mass deficit = ρ × 2h × 0.15U∞/2 ≈ 0.110 kg/(s m)
(d) Assumptions: steady 2D flow, p = p∞ on all CV faces, viscous stresses on CV boundary negligible; limitation e.g. tunnel wall effects or rake resolution
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Take a rectangular control volume per unit span. The upstream face is far ahead where u = U∞ and p = p∞, the downstream face cuts the wake where p has returned to p∞, and the two side faces are parallel to the freestream and far enough out that u ≈ U∞ there. The aerofoil is inside the CV and exerts force −D′ (in x) on the fluid.
Mass: inflow ρU∞H across the upstream face (height H) exceeds the outflow ρ∫u dy across the downstream face. The difference, ṁ_side = ρ∫(U∞ − u)dy, must leave through the side faces, carrying x-velocity U∞.
x-momentum (steady, pressures all p∞ so no net pressure force, viscous stresses on the boundary negligible):
−D′ = [ρ∫u² dy + U∞ ρ∫(U∞ − u)dy] − ρU∞²H.
Writing ρU∞²H = ρ∫U∞² dy over the same height and collecting terms:
−D′ = ρ∫[u² + U∞² − U∞u − U∞²]dy = −ρ∫u(U∞ − u)dy, so D′ = ρ∫u(U∞ − u)dy (only the wake contributes).

(b) The velocity deficit is U∞ − u = 0.15U∞(1 − |y|/h), a triangle of peak 4.5 m/s and base 2h = 0.04 m. Its integral is ½ × 0.04 × 4.5 = 0.09 m²/s, so the mass-flow deficit is 1.225 × 0.09 ≈ 0.110 kg/s per metre span.

(c) Let ε = 0.15(1 − |y|/h). Then u(U∞ − u) = U∞²(1 − ε)ε. Using s = 1 − |y|/h:
∫u(U∞ − u)dy = 2hU∞² ∫₀¹(0.15s − 0.0225s²)ds = 2hU∞²(0.075 − 0.0075) = 2 × 0.02 × 900 × 0.0675 = 2.43 m³/s².
D′ = 1.225 × 2.43 ≈ 2.98 N/m.
Cd = D′/(½ρU∞²c) = 2.98/(0.5 × 1.225 × 900 × 0.20) = 2.98/110.25 ≈ 0.027.

(d) Assumptions: steady, two-dimensional flow; static pressure equal to p∞ on every face of the CV (so the rake must be far enough downstream); negligible viscous shear on the CV boundary. Limitations: tunnel walls constrain the flow (blockage), the rake samples only at discrete points so the wake must be resolved finely, and Pitot probes give time-averaged values that can be biased in an unsteady or turbulent wake.
